claims.text: Ten hours of mechanical alloying produces high chemical homogeneity in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi powder.
CoCrFeNiTi is prone to brittle HCP formation during conventional casting or prolonged sintering because of titanium's large atomic radius.
Oxygen introduced during processing can promote Ti-containing oxide formation.
High-energy mechanical alloying followed by rapid SPS suppresses porosity in CoCrFeNiTi.
SPS at 1100–1200 °C with heating rates above 100 °C/min stabilizes a nanocrystalline, FCC-dominant solid solution containing minor BCC in CoCrFeNiTi.
Rapid SPS kinetically suppresses brittle HCP and intermetallic phase formation.
A high-purity argon atmosphere with less than 1 ppm oxygen and rapid SPS suppresses significant TiOx formation.
Controlling displacement rate during sintering minimizes thermal-expansion mismatch stresses and microcracking.
High configurational entropy stabilizes the proposed FCC-dominant dual-phase microstructure.
Nanoscale milling defects pin grain boundaries and stabilize the nanocrystalline structure.
The grain boundaries and lattice distortion generated by mechanical alloying enhance grain-boundary and solid-solution strengthening.
Rapid densification eliminates porosity before phase decomposition occurs.
The proposed process produces a grain size below 100 nm.
The processed CoCrFeNiTi alloy will have hardness above 600 HV.
The processed CoCrFeNiTi alloy will have compressive yield strength above 1500 MPa.
The processed material will contain no detectable HCP phase or significant TiOx inclusions.
Conventionally cast CoCrFeNiTi is porous and has a soft single-phase FCC structure with hardness below 300 HV.
Keeping the sintering temperature at or below 1250 °C prevents grain coarsening and HCP formation.
Limiting milling to 10 hours prevents excessive carbide or oxide contamination from the milling media.
Minimal indentation-load dependence identifies solute strengthening, whereas Hall–Petch scaling identifies grain-refinement strengthening.

contradictions.description: The mechanism attributes hardness to both solid-solution and grain-boundary strengthening, but the falsification rule frames solute strengthening as an alternative that would invalidate the proposed grain-refinement mechanism.

The predicted hardness is above 600 HV, while hardness falsification is triggered only below 500 HV, leaving results from 500 to 600 HV inconsistent with the prediction but not classified as falsifying.
